hints: Look closely at the trigger in the stem: antibodies are made against an enzyme found in some organs of your own body, not against something from outside.
Recall what we call it when the immune system treats a normal body protein as foreign, and ask yourself if that type of disease can spread from person to person.
walkthrough:
**Spot what the antigen really is**

Great start, let's read the stem like a detective. The antibodies are produced against an enzyme found in some organs of the body.

That means the antigen is part of self, not a bacterium or virus from outside.

**Link self-attack to auto-immunity**

When lymphocytes fail to recognise self and make antibodies against our own proteins, that is the definition of an auto-immune disease.

So statement 2 is true, and statement 3 is also true because that own enzyme is acting as a self-antigen.

**Decide if it is infectious**

A non-infectious disease is one you cannot catch from another person, like diabetes or cancer. Auto-immune attack comes from inside your own immune system.

So statement 1 is true as well. That gives 1, 2 and 3, which is option A.

options.A: All three are true. It is non-infectious, it is auto-immune, and antibodies are made against a self-antigen (the body's own enzyme).
options.B: This misses out statement 3, but the body's own enzyme is exactly what a self-antigen is.
options.C: This misses out statement 2, but making antibodies against self is the definition of auto-immune disease.
options.D: This misses out statement 1, but auto-immune diseases are not transmissible so they are non-infectious.
